title: Shades of Meaning
keyIdea: Some words mean nearly the same thing but not quite. These are shades of meaning. Verbs can show different ways of doing an action: tiptoe, march and sprint are all ways to move. Adjectives can be weaker or stronger: big, huge, gigantic. Some verbs show how sure someone is: know, think, wonder. Choosing the exact shade paints a sharper picture.

kid: Walk, tiptoe, march and sprint all mean moving on your feet. But they are not the same. Tiptoe is soft and slow. Sprint is as fast as you can go.
Some words get stronger and stronger. Warm, hot, scorching. Damp, wet, soaked. Each one is more than the one before.
Toss, throw and hurl all send a ball up in the air. A toss is soft. A hurl is very hard. Nibble and gobble are both eating, but in tiny or big bites.
Pick the word that fits best. A tiny mouse scurries. A giant stomps. The right word helps people see it.
adult: Shades of meaning are small differences between words that are close in meaning (near-synonyms). Common Core asks kindergarteners to tell apart verbs for the same general action, such as walk, march, strut and prance, by acting them out. In Grade 1 they compare verbs that differ in manner (look, peek, glance, stare, glare) and adjectives that differ in strength (large, gigantic). In Grade 2 it is closely related verbs (toss, throw, hurl) and adjectives (thin, slender, skinny, scrawny). In Grade 3 it is words for degrees of certainty (knew, believed, suspected, heard, wondered).

There are two kinds of shade. Verbs often differ in manner: how the action is done, how fast, how loud, how hard. Adjectives often differ in intensity: how much of the quality there is. Lining words up from weakest to strongest on a scale, sometimes called a word ladder or semantic gradient, makes the differences visible.

Common mistakes: treating synonyms as exact swaps, so a child writes 'the mouse stomped'; thinking a longer or fancier word is always stronger; mixing up glance (a quick look) with stare (a long look) and glare (an angry look); and reading 'I think' as being as sure as 'I know'. Acting the words out, and checking clues in the sentence such as tiny, hungry or asleep, fixes most of these.

In the lab your child names three walkers by how they move, orders three sets of words on a strength staircase, pulls back a ball to act out toss, throw and hurl, drops the best verb into four sentences, and places know, think and wonder on a sure-o-meter.

familyTip: Play 'Act it out': call out a verb such as walk, then a stronger or different shade such as stomp, tiptoe, stroll or sprint, and act each one together. Then try a ladder at dinner: 'Is this soup warm, hot or scorching?'

visual.caption: Is each word a gentle shade or a strong shade? Drag each word, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: name the walkers, build strength stairs, toss and hurl a ball, fill gaps and rate how sure.

practice.hint: Picture each one. Which is the biggest of all?
practice.explain: Gigantic is the strongest. Big, then huge, then gigantic: each one is bigger than the last.

practice.prompt: The baby is asleep, so {n} children ___ past the door. Which word fits best?
practice.hint: They must not wake the baby. Which way of moving is quiet?
practice.explain: Tiptoe fits best. The {n} children need quiet steps so the baby stays asleep. Stomping and racing are loud.

practice.prompt: Mia throws the ball as hard and far as she can. Which word fits?
practice.hint: Which word means a very hard throw?
practice.explain: Hurls fits. A hurl is a very hard throw. A toss is soft, and a drop is not a throw at all.

practice.prompt: The puppy ate all {n} biscuits in big, fast bites. Which word fits best?
practice.hint: Big, fast bites. Is that nibbling or gobbling?
practice.explain: Gobbled fits. Gobble means eating fast in big bites. Nibble is tiny bites, and you sip a drink.

pool.prompt: Put these in order from least wet to most wet: wet, soaked, damp.
pool.hint: Which is only a little bit wet?
pool.explain: Damp is a little wet, wet is more, and soaked is wet all the way through.

pool.prompt: Which word means a quick look?
pool.hint: One of these takes only a second.
pool.explain: Glance is a quick look. Stare is a long look, and glare is an angry look.

pool.prompt: The {n} soldiers move in step, knees up, left, right, left. What are they doing?
pool.hint: Big, even steps in time together.
pool.explain: Marching is big, steady steps in time, like the {n} soldiers. Tiptoeing is quiet, and strolling is slow and relaxed.

pool.prompt: Which sentence shows the speaker is most sure?
choices: I wonder if it is Tuesday.
pool.explain: Know is the most sure. Think is fairly sure, and wonder is not sure at all.

pool.prompt: It is so hot on the beach that the sand burns your feet. Which word fits best?
pool.hint: Sand that burns is more than a bit hot.
pool.explain: Scorching fits, because it means very, very hot. Warm is only a bit hot.

pool.prompt: Dad gently throws {n} beanbags to the baby, soft and short. What does he do?
pool.hint: Soft and short. Which verb is the gentle one?
pool.explain: He tosses the {n} beanbags. A toss is gentle and short. Hurl and fling are hard throws.

pool.hint: Which one is even smaller than small?
pool.explain: Tiny is the smallest. Small and little are close, but tiny means very small.
